author: reek
body: A server that serves one caller and goes back to accept must be able to take the next caller. This is the test for the half of the problem that a single-connection server hits, and it needs no NIC, no VM and no second guest: the whole defect is expressible against `tcp-step` and `net-session-owns-segment`, which are pure.

author: reek
body: THE DEFECT. `tcp-set-state` carries every field forward, including `remote-port`, and `tcp-step-closed`'s `EvListen` arm reaches `TcpListening` through it. So a listener that has once been claimed by a peer still names that peer after it closes and re-listens. The demux check then reads a fresh caller's SYN as somebody else's traffic and drops it, and the server waits forever for a request that was on the wire. A listener has no peer by definition; `remote-port = 0` is the sentinel `net-session-owns-segment` already keys on for exactly this.

author: reek
body: THE CONTROLS ARE THE TEST. `second-caller-admitted` fails against the unfixed code and is the point, but on its own it cannot tell a fixed demux from a deleted one -- removing the remote-port check entirely makes it pass. `claimed-rejects-stranger` is what pins the check still doing its job: once a peer has claimed the listener, another peer's frame must still be refused. A change that satisfies one and not both is wrong, in whichever direction it fails.

author: reek
body: A listener as a server actually builds one: no peer named, because it does not know who will call.

author: reek
body: One whole connection, from the SYN that claims the listener to the close and the re-listen that a serve loop performs before taking the next caller.
